extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent applicants, and IP practitioners (especially those handling AI-related inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examination standards for handling patent applications involving AI/ML technologies at the Japan Patent Office, including how to assess description requirements, inventive step, classification, and the legal status of inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Case examples aim to help provide a clear understanding of examination decisions from the viewpoint of the description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO published case examples of AI-related technologies to clarify how the description requirement applies to AI inventions; see provided links for concrete examples and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step is a central examination criterion for AI-related inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The JPO's case examples illustrate how inventive step is evaluated in various AI/ML situations (e.g., mere application of AI, modification or preprocessing of training data). Examiners should consult these examples when determining inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere application/systemization of AI does not itself confer inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Mere application of AI’ and ‘Mere systemization using AI’ are shown as situations where inventive step is not necessarily present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case Examples (e.g., Claim 1 and Claim 2 in Example 34) indicate that simply automating or systemizing an operation using AI, without more, will not establish an inventive step. Examiners should look for technical contribution beyond applying AI as a tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification of training data requires a significant training/learning effect to be inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Modification of training data for machine learning that is a mere combination of known data and does not show a significant effect is not identified as inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case Example 35 indicates that adding or modifying training data must produce a demonstrable, significant training/learning effect to support inventive step; otherwise it may be treated as an obvious/data-management change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding training data can produce a significant training/learning effect (possible inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some case examples, significant training/learning effects by adding data are highlighted as relevant to inventive-step assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where adding data meaningfully changes model behavior or achieves a non-obvious technical effect, examiners should consider that as evidence supporting inventive step (see Case Example 33/34 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-processing of training data may be a technical contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-processing of training data for machine learning is specifically discussed in case examples (Case Example 36) in relation to inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether preprocessing steps provide a technical solution/effect beyond routine data handling; such effects may support inventive step if non-obvious and technically motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of AI-related inventions (G06N)
rubrics_metrics.description: G06N: A patent classification assigned to inventions related to computer systems based on specific calculation models, which mainly describes AI technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use G06N classification to identify and track AI-related patent applications; JPO uses this class when reporting application trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case examples as an interpretive tool
rubrics_metrics.description: JPO created and published case examples of AI-related technologies to help provide a clear understanding of examination decisions (description requirement, inventive step, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and applicants should consult the JPO case examples (including the newly added 2019 examples and linked documents) to understand how principles are applied in practice; links and PDFs are provided by JPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary/expert consultation for AI examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO inaugurated a Team for Supporting AI Examinations to collect and share knowledge on the latest AI technologies and case examples, and to provide consultation services to examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI examination should involve cross-technical-field collaboration and consultation with AI experts to realize efficient, highest-quality examinations; the Team shares knowledge via study meetings and policy review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of examination standards for accessibility (manga/guidelines/videos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic concept of Examination Standards has been introduced in Manga form (AI/IoT edition) to explain characteristic determination aspects and basic concepts regarding patent examinations common to all fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO publishes accessible explanatory materials (manga, English translations, and chapter videos) to help examiners and stakeholders understand examination concepts and characteristic determinations for AI/IoT technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must be a natural person (legal requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art.36(1) of the Patent Act is interpreted to mean the 'shimei (name)' of the inventor must be a natural person; indicating a non-natural person (e.g., machines including AI) in the inventor column is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO interpretation: inventor = natural person with the right to obtain a patent; this interpretation aligns with provisions in Arts. 29(1), 33(1), and 34(1). Applicants cannot list AI/machines as inventors; rights may be transferred prior to filing according to existing law.
